'''Richard''' '''Hadley Holm''' (September 24, 1933 – February 15, 2021)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=RICHARD HOLM Obituary - (1933 - 2021) - Cambridge, MA - Boston Globe|url=https://www.legacy.com/amp/obituaries/bostonglobe/197803149|access-date=2021-02-22|website=www.legacy.com|language=en}}</ref> was an American [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic chemist]].

==Biography==
A native of [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]],<ref name=":0" /> Holm received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] from the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]] in 1955<ref name=":0" /> and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1959 under the direction of [[F. Albert Cotton]].<ref>[http://www.chemistry.msu.edu/Genealogy/chem_gene.shtml Chemical genealogy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170530210821/http://www2.chemistry.msu.edu/Genealogy/chem_gene.shtml |date=May 30, 2017 }}, Michigan State U. chemistry dept.</ref><ref name=":2">[http://library.stanford.edu/depts/swain/history/mosher/biography.html Stanford Chemistry Dept. History 1977–2000: Professors, Brief Biographical Summaries] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212205847/http://library.stanford.edu/depts/swain/history/mosher/biography.html |date=2012-02-12 }}, Stanford U.</ref> As an independent researcher, he joined the chemistry faculty at [[Harvard University]] in 1962. He was later on the faculties of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and [[Stanford University]] prior to returning to Harvard in 1980.<ref name=":2"/> He was the Higgins Professor of Chemistry at Harvard.

== Research ==
Holm's research encompassed [[Chemical synthesis|synthetic]], [[Chemical structure|structural]], and [[reactivity (chemistry)|reactivity]] aspects of [[Transition state|transition]] [[Chemical element|element]] chemistry. He was best known for the preparations of the first synthetic analogs of the active sites of [[Iron-sulfur cluster|iron-sulfur proteins]].<ref>{{citation|author1=Herskovitz, T. |author2=Averill, B. A. |author3=Holm, R. H. |author4=Ibers, J. A. |author5=Phillips, W. D. |author6=Weiher, J. F.  |name-list-style=amp |title=Structure and properties of a synthetic analogue of bacterial iron-sulfur proteins|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]|year=1972|volume=69|issue=9|pages=2437–2441|doi=10.1073/pnas.69.9.2437|pmc=426959|pmid=4506765|bibcode=1972PNAS...69.2437H |doi-access=free }}.</ref> These discoveries were significant in the development of [[bioinorganic chemistry]]. He continued his work in the field of iron-sulfur clusters until the end, examining the active sites of the enzymes [[nitrogenase]] and [[carbon monoxide dehydrogenase]]. Additionally, his interests included the [[biomimetic synthesis|biomimetic]] chemistry of [[molybdenum]]- and [[tungsten]]-containing oxo-transferases.

== Awards ==
His accomplishments were honored with numerous awards including the [[NAS Award in Chemical Sciences|National Academy of Sciences Award in Chemical Sciences]].<ref>National Academy of Sciences. [http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_chemical_sciences NAS Award in Chemical Sciences] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229180055/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_chemical_sciences|date=2010-12-29}}, Accessed on October 18, 2007.</ref> and the [[F. Albert Cotton#F.A. Cotton Medal for Excellence in Chemical Research|F.A. Cotton Medal for Excellence in Chemical Research]] of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 2005. He was a member of [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. He is the co-recipient of the 2016 [[Welch Award in Chemistry]] along with [[Stephen J. Lippard]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Welch|date=2021-05-17|title=Richard H. Holm|url=https://www.welch1.org/awards/welch-award-in-chemistry/recipients/richard-h-holm|access-date=2021-05-17|website=Welch|language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Holm met his future wife Florence while he was in college at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]], where they were [[Pen pal|pen-pals]]. They married upon her graduation. Holm is survived by his wife, their four children, Sharon, Eric Richard, Christian, and Marg, and five grandchildren.<ref name=":0" />
